The question this page answers

Which providers are evidenced, under whose authority, and what do we actually know about their status?

Providers: official lists show formal status on a date; operation needs other evidence

The list of licensed banks issued by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), as checked on 7 September 2026, names 26 banks, and its 2026 exchange and remittance roster lists 98 exchange companies, 225 individual exchange establishments and 106 remittance agents. These sources show who holds which formal status under that authority on a stated date. Operation, activity, reach and service quality require additional evidence.

How numbers are presented

Every consequential number stays attached to its unit, scope, time and limitation. Evidence measured at different times is never presented as if it described the same moment.

Explore questionsOpen evidence
What this does not establish

What provider evidence does not establish

Listing or licensing is not operation. A provider count is not a branch or service-point count. A dated negative or enforcement event is not a permanent status. A named set of providers covered by the evidence does not establish activity, market share, client reach, service quality or inclusion outcomes without additional evidence.

What we still do not know

What we still do not know well enough

The 2026 exchange and remittance roster can be counted by source category, but this resource still lacks a fully reconciled view of current operation across all provider classes. The main open questions are entity deduplication across categories, reconciliation of the 2026 enforcement decisions (dated January–September 2026) with the roster, wallet-universe comparability, dated operating status and verified service geography.

03Scope

Whose list is this?

The provider lists and status decisions on this page come from instruments issued by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden); the bank list was checked on 7 September 2026. Since 2016 central-bank authority has been divided, and some banks on that list have addresses in Sana'a and Taiz in the source. Status under any other authority is not established here; this defines the scope of the evidence and is not a judgement about either authority. Absence from a CBY-Aden list does not show that a provider is unlicensed elsewhere, and presence on it does not show that a provider can operate across all of Yemen.

04Evidence

Banks: a dated formal roster, not an operating census

The list of licensed banks issued by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), as checked on 7 September 2026, names 26 banks; 12 of them are classified as microfinance banks on the basis of their names in the source. These are facts about formal listing and classification. They do not establish whether every institution is operating, which branches are active, what products are available, market share, payment-rail participation or underserved-client reach.

Another view of the evidence
05Analysis

Exchange and remittance: the 2026 roster is countable; operation remains a separate question

The official 2026 roster of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) lists 98 exchange companies, 225 individual exchange establishments and 106 remittance agents. These are three source-defined categories, not a deduplicated total of unique firms. The 2026 suspension, withdrawal or closure decisions are separate status evidence: they are dated January–September 2026, some were issued before the roster and some after it, and the roster’s own issue date is not stated. They have to be reconciled entity by entity before any count of providers operating on a given date is stated.

06Analysis

Status events update an entity; they do not create the market denominator

Licence withdrawal, suspension and other enforcement decisions in 2026 are dated events for named entities and belong on each provider's status history. Because the annual roster and the 2026 decisions refer to different dates and require entity-level matching, this resource does not mechanically subtract the decisions from the 2026 roster to produce a count of operating providers. Silence about another provider is not evidence that it is active or compliant.

Analysis

Wallet counts are not yet one clean provider trend

Official material from the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) reports different wallet counts at different dates and in different contexts: 7 in 2024 Q3, 9 in 2025 H1 and 8 licensed e-wallets in a September 2025 statement. This resource does not plot the sequence 7, 9, 8 as entry and exit because the definitions and the sets of wallets each source covers have not been reconciled. A June 2024 circular separately named 12 wallets, entities or services as unlicensed on that source date; that negative list cannot be carried forward as a 2026 status or used to infer the full list of licensed wallets.

System context

Where providers sit in the wider system

Provider authority and status sit upstream of access and use. A provider may be legally present but have limited operating geography; a payment or finance product may exist without evidence of active use; and an enforcement event may change formal status without telling us what happened to customer access. This resource therefore links provider status to Access, Payments, Finance and Reforms without collapsing those questions.

System structure

Money exchangers are part of the financial system, not a footnote

Historical evidence shows that money-exchange businesses have long formed a substantial part of Yemen’s financial-service landscape. That earlier evidence helps explain why exchange and remittance providers matter to the system, but it does not establish the complete set of providers operating in 2026, their operating status, branch activity or geographic reach.

What exactly do we mean by microfinance growth?
Yemen’s microfinance record does not move on one axis. Borrower counts, saver or depositor measures, nominal portfolios and institutional form are not the same measure, and they do not yet form one harmonised growth series.

What measurement would change the decision?

PriorityP0 · Providers / Geography
A register of active financial access points
Current official rosters establish selected listing, licensing and event states, but do not provide a complete, geocoded register of active branches, agents, merchants and other service points.
Evidence needed: An authoritative or jointly documented register of individual access points recording type, active status, date, location and services, plus population denominators and road-network data that allow coverage and travel distance or time to be calculated.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would distinguish listing and licensing from operation and observed access before any access or opportunity map is interpreted.
Open this measurement priority
PriorityP1 · Identity / Digital access
Digital onboarding and identity journeys
KYC and e-money rules are documented, but this resource lacks journey-level evidence on attempts, completion, rejection, abandonment, time and cost.
Evidence needed: Journey-level administrative or survey data across onboarding stages: identity and KYC verification, attempts, completion, rejection, abandonment, time and cost.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would identify where users leave or fail the onboarding journey and which frictions are associated with those points.

When was it measured or observed?The official 2026 roster (issue date not stated); 2026 enforcement decisions are separate evidence.
The official 2026 exchange and remittance roster can be counted; whether providers operate now is a separate question
The official 2026 roster of exchange and remittance providers issued by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) lists 98 exchange companies, 225 individual exchange establishments and 106 remittance agents. These are roster entries counted by the roster's own classes: the three class totals are not a count of unique providers, nor a verified count of providers operating now. Because the roster does not state its issue date, CBY-Aden's 2026 decisions (dated January to September 2026) suspending or withdrawing the licences of named entities, or closing their premises, are matched with the roster entity by entity, because a decision may or may not already be reflected in it.
Who or what does it apply to? Source-listed exchange companies, individual exchange establishments and remittance agents; entries are counted separately by the three classes used in the official roster.

When was it measured or observed?List as checked on 7 September 2026
Listing or licensing does not establish operation
The list of licensed banks of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), as checked on 7 September 2026, names 26 banks. Appearing on the list establishes listing or licensing in that source, not operation.
Who or what does it apply to? Banks named on the licensed-bank list of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden); list presence is not proof of current operation, branch footprint, product availability or market share
Open evidence record
When was it measured or observed?Decisions dated 1 January to 24 September 2026
Enforcement decisions are events, not a market census
Governor's decisions of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) dated January to September 2026 record licence withdrawals, suspensions and closures for specific exchange and remittance providers. This record covers selected CBY-Aden Governor's decisions of 2026 concerning exchange and remittance providers (Nos. 1–6, 9–11, 13–15, 17 and 18); other decision numbers are not included and their subjects are not assessed. The official 2026 roster can be counted by class, but these decisions are matched with it entity by entity and are not subtracted from it to produce a count of providers operating now.
Who or what does it apply to? Only the providers named in the decisions covered here (for Decision No. 18, the named entities have not yet been transcribed); not the full set of exchange and remittance providers

The list of licensed banks of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), as checked on 7 September 2026, names 26 banks; 12 of them are classified as microfinance banks on the basis of their names in the source. This establishes a dated listing and classification only: being listed or licensed does not mean operating, active or reaching underserved clients.
